title: Chapter 13: Lambdas, Functional Interfaces, and Optional
description: Use behavior values to simplify decisions without hiding side effects. Learners identify target functional interfaces, reason about captured state, use primitive specializations, compose method references and functions, restrict Optional to meaningful absence-return contracts, and separate a deterministic decision-making core from I/O and mutation boundaries.

lessons.title: Lambda target typing and effectively-final capture
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Lambda target typing and effectively-final capture

## A lambda implements a target
```java
java.util.function.Predicate<String> longName = text -> text.length() > 3;
System.out.println(longName.test("Java")); // true
int minimum = 4;
java.util.function.Predicate<String> enough = text -> text.length() >= minimum;
```
Predicate is a functional interface: one abstract operation, test, supplies the target parameter and return types. A lambda is not independently typed without context. Expression bodies return their expression; block bodies use return when a value is required.

Captured local variables must be final or effectively final. Reassigning minimum after capture makes the code invalid. A captured reference can still point to a mutable object, so this rule does not make lambdas pure or thread-safe. In a lambda, this refers to the enclosing instance.

## Practice
Write predicates for empty, uppercase, and minimum-length strings with a defined null policy. Replace a mutable captured counter with an explicit result calculation. Explain why a lambda changing a captured list can compile while still causing a race under concurrent execution.

exercises.title: Lambda target typing and effectively-final capture: concept check
choices: Reassignment of any variable declared inside the lambda body
hints: Effectively-final only forbids reassigning the captured local variable itself; it says nothing about mutating an object that the variable refers to.

lessons.title: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, and primitive variants
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, and primitive variants

## Pick the interface by data flow
Predicate<T> maps T to boolean. Function<T,R> maps T to R. Consumer<T> performs an action without a result. Supplier<T> produces T without an argument. UnaryOperator<T> and BinaryOperator<T> preserve the value type.

```java
java.util.function.Function<String,Integer> length = String::length;
java.util.function.Predicate<Integer> positive = n -> n > 0;
java.util.function.Supplier<java.util.ArrayList<String>> fresh =
    java.util.ArrayList::new;
System.out.println(positive.test(length.apply("Java"))); // true
```
Primitive specializations such as IntUnaryOperator avoid wrapper types in numeric operations. Consumer does not imply purity; it commonly marks a side effect. A Supplier can return a new value each time or a shared value, so its lifecycle contract must be documented.

## Practice
Choose an interface for parsing a line, generating an ID, sending an email, checking authorization, and combining two totals. Explain why a predicate that secretly changes account state violates reasonable caller expectations. Build a retry helper only after specifying whether repeated Supplier calls are safe; “no arguments” does not imply idempotency.

exercises.title: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, and primitive variants: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Which interface describes an input-to-result transformation?
hints: Function<T,R>'s single abstract method takes an input and produces a transformed result, unlike Consumer (no result) or Runnable (no input or result).

lessons.title: Method references, function composition, and readability
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Method references, function composition, and readability

## References abbreviate compatible calls
String::trim is an unbound instance reference: the argument supplies the receiver. System.out::println binds a receiver already known. Integer::parseInt references a static method. ArrayList::new references construction.

```java
java.util.function.Function<String,String> trim = String::trim;
java.util.function.Function<String,Integer> size = String::length;
var trimmedLength = trim.andThen(size);
System.out.println(trimmedLength.apply(" Java ")); // 4
```
andThen applies the left function first; compose applies the supplied function first. Reversing order can change results or make types incompatible. Predicate.and/or short-circuit just like boolean operators, so side effects can make composition order observable.

## Readability boundary
A method reference should clarify a familiar operation. Long generic chains with unclear intermediate types are often easier to maintain as named methods. Bound method references capture an object immediately; consider whether that object can be null or retained longer than intended.

## Practice
Build normalize -> validate -> length as named stages. Predict the type after each stage. Compose a trim function with a null-handling wrapper and explain which stage must execute first. Compare a reference with its equivalent lambda before choosing the clearer version.

exercises.title: Method references, function composition, and readability: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: In trim.andThen(length), which operation runs first?
hints: andThen runs the function it is called on first, then feeds that result into the argument function, so trim executes before length.

lessons.title: Optional map, flatMap, fallback, and API design
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Optional map, flatMap, fallback, and API design

## Optional communicates a missing result
```java
java.util.Optional<String> found = java.util.Optional.ofNullable(rawName);
String display = found.map(String::trim)
    .filter(name -> !name.isEmpty())
    .orElse("Anonymous");
```
map transforms a present value; flatMap uses a function that already returns Optional and avoids nesting. filter can turn a present value into absence. orElseGet obtains a fallback lazily; orElse evaluates its argument even when a value is already present.

## Use a narrow contract
Optional is mainly useful for a return value that may legitimately be missing. Return an empty collection for zero results rather than Optional<List<T>> unless absence has a separate meaning. Do not return null instead of Optional.empty. get without a presence guarantee simply relocates a possible failure.

Absence is not infrastructure failure: a failed database lookup must not silently become Optional.empty.

## Practice
Implement findTask and compose a lookup of its optional owner. Count fallback invocations to demonstrate orElse versus orElseGet. Use orElseThrow when the current use case requires presence, and choose a domain-meaningful exception. Explain why pervasive Optional fields complicate many serialization and persistence models.

exercises.title: Optional map, flatMap, fallback, and API design: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why use orElseGet for an expensive fallback?
choices: Its supplier runs only when the value is absent
hints: orElseGet takes a Supplier that is only invoked when the Optional is empty, while orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly whether or not a value is present.

lessons.title: Chapter 13 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 13 assessment

Before touching the debugger, use this chapter's rules on lazy versus eager Optional fallbacks to predict what **Lazy optional fallback** should print, then run it and repair the defect so the fallback supplier runs only when the value is absent.

The normalize function lab exercises one deterministic transformation in isolation; it is not proof of every competency from functional-interface selection through purity and testability covered across the chapter's five lessons. Review the repaired source and explain why orElseGet's laziness matters here, without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 13 implementation lab: normalize
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `normalize`. Return trimmed lowercase text, or UNKNOWN when the trimmed result is empty. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Use trim and toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT). Input is non-null.
hints: Trim first, then lowercase with Locale.ROOT so the emptiness check reflects the trimmed text rather than the original input.
Check an all-whitespace string, a single character, and an already-empty string before submitting.

exercises.title: Lazy optional fallback
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the fallback call so the side-effecting fallback() supplier runs only when the Optional is actually empty, and the program writes exactly `ready:0`. Keep the same call counter and explain why orElse's eager evaluation caused the extra call, rather than hard-coding the print statement. Output tests verify the printed result; confirming the supplier truly stayed lazy requires reading the source.
hints: Use a lazy supplier when the fallback has work or side effects.
